subject: BATTERSBY and GLENNER (1961)
object: BATTERSBY and GLENNER (1961) reported on familial cardiomyopathy.

subject: KARIV et al. (1964)
object: KARIV et al. (1964) described familial cardiomyopathy, with special attention to electrocardiographic and vectorcardiographic findings.

subject: Goldblatt et al. (1987)
object: Goldblatt et al. (1987) described idiopathic, isolated dilated cardiomyopathy in 3 members of a consanguineous Madeira Portuguese family.

subject: Goldblatt et al. (1987)
object: Goldblatt et al. (1987) concluded that dilated cardiomyopathy in a consanguineous Madeira Portuguese family was inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern. They noted that familial isolated dilated cardiomyopathy is usually reported as autosomal dominant with variable penetrance and expressivity. After reviewing the literature, they suggested that the autosomal recessive form is more common than previously reported.

subject: Goldblatt et al. (1987)
object: Goldblatt et al. (1987) noted that cardiomyopathy is a heterogeneous disorder with many inherited and acquired causes.

subject: Seliem et al. (2000)
object: Seliem et al. (2000) evaluated 55 consecutive cases of dilated cardiomyopathy diagnosed by echocardiography in patients younger than 10 years of age, seen over a 5-year period in the Eastern Province of Saudi Arabia. They came from 41 families of Arab descent and made up 20% of the offspring of those families. In 95% of cases, age at presentation was under 30 months (range, 1 to 100 months); 38% were male and 62% female.

subject: Seliem et al. (2000)
object: In the series of Seliem et al. (2000), 25 patients (46%) died, 15 (27%) improved, and 15 (27%) recovered. At diagnosis, the left ventricular shortening fraction ranged from 5 to 28% and did not differ among the patients who died, improved, or recovered.

subject: Seliem et al. (2000)
object: Seliem et al. (2000) found that the parents were first cousins in 19 of the 41 families (46%), with no obvious consanguinity in the other 22 (54%). A complex segregation analysis of the family data using the mixed model of inheritance showed that recessive inheritance fit the data best. The authors suggested that recessive dilated cardiomyopathy may be hard to recognize in populations where consanguineous marriage is uncommon and families have few children.

subject: Murphy et al. (2004)
object: Murphy et al. (2004) screened the cardiac troponin I gene (TNNI3) in 235 patients with dilated cardiomyopathy, using mutation analysis suitable for identifying both dominant and recessive mutations, and identified a novel TNNI3 mutation in a family with recessive disease. The authors stated that TNNI3 was the first recessive gene identified for this condition.

subject: Murphy et al. (2004)
object: Murphy et al. (2004) found in functional studies that the recessive TNNI3 mutation impaired troponin interactions, which they suggested could lead to diminished myocardial contractility.

subject: Murphy et al. (2004)
object: Murphy et al. (2004) suggested that other recessive genes for idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy could be identified by mutation analyses designed to detect homozygous mutations.

subject: Carballo et al. (2009)
object: Carballo et al. (2009) screened 96 probands with dilated cardiomyopathy for TNNI3 mutations and reported the first autosomal dominant DCM-causing mutations in TNNI3. This adds TNNI3 to the genes in which different mutations can cause either hypertrophic or dilated cardiomyopathy.

subject: Carballo et al. (2009)
object: Carballo et al. (2009) described 5 carriers of TNNI3 mutations from families with severe, early-onset familial dilated cardiomyopathy. Three of the 5 needed cardiac transplantation, at ages 6, 15, and 24 years.

subject: Carballo et al. (2009)
object: Carballo et al. (2009) used heteroduplex analysis and sequencing to identify a novel TNNI3 missense mutation, lys36-to-gln (K36Q), in a family with severe, early-onset dilated cardiomyopathy. The variant was evaluated by segregation analysis and in normal controls. Troponin reconstituted with the mutant troponin I gave a lower maximum ATPase rate and lower Ca(2+) sensitivity than wildtype, and mutant thin filaments had reduced Ca(2+) affinity.

subject: TNNI3 p.K36Q
object: TNNI3

subject: Carballo et al. (2009)
object: Carballo et al. (2009) identified a second novel TNNI3 missense mutation, asn185-to-lys (N185K), in a family with severe, early-onset familial dilated cardiomyopathy. In functional studies, troponin containing the mutant troponin I gave a lower maximum actin-tropomyosin-activated myosin ATPase rate and lower Ca(2+) sensitivity than wildtype, and mutant thin filaments had reduced Ca(2+) affinity.

subject: TNNI3 p.N185K
object: TNNI3

subject: Carballo et al. (2009)
object: Carballo et al. (2009) noted that the functional changes caused by the TNNI3 mutations, lower ATPase rates and reduced Ca(2+) sensitivity, closely matched a consistent phenotype seen with proven DCM mutations in other thin filament proteins. They took this as support that the mutations are disease-causing.
